body.statement: For every fixed \(K\ge2\), \(q\in\mathbb R^K\), and positive \(R_g,R_e\), \(\lim_{T\to\infty}V_{T,K}(q;R_g,R_e)=V_{\infty,K}(q;R_g,R_e)=R_e^2N_q^2\). For every power of two \(L\ge2d\), \(D_L^{\mathrm G}\in\mathfrak D_{\infty}\), it has at most \(2L^2\) hidden states, and \(\mathcal R_{\infty,K}(D_L^{\mathrm G})=\max\{R_e^2N_q^2,(R_g^2/L)\lambda_{\max}(D_q(M_L+H_d)D_q^{\top})\}\). Consequently, if \(L\ge\max\{2d,B_KR_g^2/R_e^2\}\), then \(\mathcal R_{\infty,K}(D_L^{\mathrm G})=R_e^2N_q^2\).
body.justification: This theorem identifies the global stationary efficiency frontier and supplies a finite-state optimal randomization with a matching spectral lower bound.
body.gap: Tellambura, Guo, and Barton use two deterministic complementary inputs for an information criterion; no checked result proves one-path design-based minimax MSE or equality with the finite-horizon limit.
body.consumer: It gives an implementable long-horizon binary assignment law for individualized impulse-response experiments when treatment counts may remain random.
body.proof_tex:
We first verify feasibility and finite-state complexity.  The random uniform phase in \(\texttt{def:golay-block-law}\) makes \(D_L^{\mathrm G}\) invariant under a unit shift.  The one- and two-point calculations in \(\texttt{lem:golay-tensor-certificate}\) give global sign symmetry and zero off-origin autocorrelation, so \(D_L^{\mathrm G}\in\mathfrak D_\infty\) by \(\texttt{def:stationary-design-class}\).  More explicitly, global negation corresponds to replacing every independent block sign by its negative, which preserves their joint law.  A hidden state may be taken as
\[
(r,\alpha,\sigma)\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}\times\mathbb F_2^p\times\{-1,+1\}.
\]
For \(r<L-1\) the phase advances deterministically, and at \(r=L-1\) a fresh independent uniform \((\alpha,\sigma)\) is drawn and the phase returns to zero.  The uniform distribution on these \(2L^2\) states is invariant and emits exactly the random-phase block law, proving the asserted complexity bound.

For a fixed such \(L\), combine \(\texttt{lem:zero-prehistory-asymptotics}\) with the covariance limit in \(\texttt{lem:golay-tensor-certificate}\).  Continuity of the largest eigenvalue gives
\[
T\mathbb E[u_Tu_T^{\top}]
\longrightarrow \frac1L D_q(M_L+H_d)D_q^{\top}.
\tag{16}
\]
The same zero-prehistory lemma gives
\[
T^2\|F_{T,q}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\longrightarrow N_q^2.
\tag{17}
\]
Every finite restriction of the stationary law belongs to \(\mathfrak D_T\).  Hence \(\texttt{lem:exact-risk-reduction}\), (16), (17), and the definition of stationary risk imply the exact formula
\[
\mathcal R_{\infty,K}(D_L^{\mathrm G})
=\max\!\left\{R_e^2N_q^2,\frac{R_g^2}{L}
\lambda_{\max}\bigl(D_q(M_L+H_d)D_q^{\top}\bigr)\right\}.
\tag{18}
\]

We now certify when the second block cannot exceed the first.  From the definition of \(D_q\), the inequality \((a+b)^2\leq2a^2+2b^2\), and a count over the two possible shifts,
\[
\|D_q\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\leq\|D_q\|_{\mathrm F}^2
\leq2\sum_{j=0}^{d}\bigl((d-j)+j\bigr)q_j^2
=2d\|q\|_2^2.
\tag{19}
\]
Parseval's identity gives
\[
\|q\|_2^2=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|Q_q(e^{i\omega})|^2\,d\omega
\leq N_q^2.
\tag{20}
\]
The autocorrelation estimate proved in \(\texttt{lem:golay-tensor-certificate}\) is valid also at \(d=L/2\), so for every \(L\geq2d\), equations (7), (19), and (20) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_{\max}\bigl(D_q(M_L+H_d)D_q^{\top}\bigr)
&\leq \|D_q\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\operatorname{tr}(M_L+H_d)\\
&\leq2dN_q^2\sum_{h=1}^{d}(h^2+h)
=B_KN_q^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
\]
Thus if \(L\geq B_KR_g^2/R_e^2\), positivity of \(R_e\) and (21) show that the signal term in (18) is at most \(R_e^2N_q^2\).  Equation (18) then proves exact attainment of the noise floor.  This also covers \(q=0\), when both terms vanish.

It remains to prove that this floor is globally minimax and is the finite-horizon limit.  For every \(D\in\mathfrak D_T\), \(\texttt{lem:exact-risk-reduction}\) gives the design-independent lower bound
\[
\mathcal R_T(D)\geq T^2R_e^2\|F_{T,q}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2.
\]
Taking the infimum and using (17) yields
\[
\liminf_{T\to\infty}V_{T,K}(q;R_g,R_e)\geq R_e^2N_q^2.
\tag{22}
\]
Choose one power of two \(L\) satisfying the two displayed lower bounds in the theorem.  Its restriction is feasible for every \(T\), so
\[
V_{T,K}(q;R_g,R_e)\leq\mathcal R_T(D_L^{\mathrm G}|_{1:T}).
\]
The right side converges by (16)--(18) to \(R_e^2N_q^2\), proving the reverse \(\limsup\) inequality and hence
\[
\lim_{T\to\infty}V_{T,K}(q;R_g,R_e)=R_e^2N_q^2.
\tag{23}
\]
For any \(P_\infty\in\mathfrak D_\infty\), the same design-independent lower bound and (17) imply
\(\mathcal R_{\infty,K}(P_\infty)\geq R_e^2N_q^2\).  The chosen \(D_L^{\mathrm G}\) attains equality by (18)--(21).  Taking the stationary infimum proves
\[
V_{\infty,K}(q;R_g,R_e)=R_e^2N_q^2,
\]
which together with (23) establishes the stated equality of finite-horizon and stationary limits.
